title: Transcript: Nepal PM Balen Shah’s Speech At UN General Assembly 81st Session - singjupost.com
description: Transcript: Nepal PM Balen Shah’s Speech At UN General Assembly 81st Session  singjupost.com
publisher.title: singjupost.com
full_article:
EDITOR’S NOTE: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah addressed the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly following the devastating Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods that struck Nepal’s mountain communities weeks earlier. In his address, he called on the international community to recognize the disaster as a warning about the climate crisis, and urged reform of global systems of finance, trade, and cooperation to ensure genuine climate justice for vulnerable nations like Nepal.

TRANSCRIPT:

A Warning From the Himalayas

BALENDRA SHAH: Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, excellencies, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen, I come before you from Nepal, a distant country in the Himalayas, carrying a close warning for humanity. I wish I could stand here today simply to talk about development, democracy, peace, and the hopes of a new young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportion, about families waiting for loved ones who will never come home, about communities searching through the mud, rocks, and water for people whose bodies may never be recovered, about bridges, about roads, schools, homes, and livelihoods swept away in minutes. About a country whose steady progress to achieve Sustainable Development Goals has been interrupted. Four weeks ago, the world saw shocking images of catastrophic flash floods that swept away Nepal’s mountain communities with ferocity many have called a “mountain tsunami” or “Himalayan tsunami.”

The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy. It was a warning to the world, and I ask you today, “have you really heard that warning?” Nearly three years ago, standing in the shadow of Mount Everest, the Secretary-General of the United Nations warned humanity about the madness of impending climate disaster. That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard loudly enough. We in Nepal heard it.

Our communities heard it. Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it with evidence. But we, the political leaders, have been negligent in translating those warnings into action at the speed and scale that vulnerable people require. Last month, we saw the tragic consequences: a warming climate that is destabilizing the fragile Himalayan ecology, melting permafrost that is fracturing mountain slopes beneath the glaciers, and accelerating the risk of ice-rock avalanches, floods, landslides, and other cascading hazards.

The resulting devastation unleashed havoc on both sides of Nepal’s border. The flood continued downstream into India. This tells us something fundamental. Climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports.

Gratitude and the Scale of Recovery

Excellencies, I am not here to complain, but to share some suggestions. First, I wish to express Nepal’s deep gratitude to all those who came to our aid in the aftermath of the deluge. Our immediate neighbors, India and China, offered prompt and generous assistance. Other friendly countries, the United Nations system, humanitarian agencies, philanthropies, and people around the world stood with Nepal. To all of them, I say thank you on behalf of the grateful people of Nepal.

Nepal now faces a massive task of recovery and reconstruction. After at least fourteen hundred deaths and over sixty-six thousand people still missing, a rapid assessment pegs physical recovery needs at about 10% of GDP. As in rebuilding after the 2015 Gorkha earthquake, we count on your solidarity and support. But we must also understand why this disaster matters beyond Nepal. Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it. Our glaciers are retreating. Our mountain slopes are becoming unstable. Our rivers are becoming less predictable, and every major disaster threatens to erase years of development. For Nepal, climate catastrophe is not just a humanitarian event, but a development emergency.

It destroys roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms, and livelihoods. It destroys clean energy infrastructure that we need to fuel our future, and it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause. But we are not here to blame any country or continent. We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity.

Climate Justice, Not Charity

Through the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the international community has already agreed to the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. Those who have historically contributed more to the problem and those with greater capacity to respond must do more. Climate justice cannot remain a beautiful phrase in a United Nations document. People of our country must be allowed to build their future instead of constantly rebuilding their past. Excellencies, the Hindu Kush Himalaya is home to nearly 2 billion people.

These mountains provide water, ecosystems, agriculture, and livelihoods to populations far beyond Nepal. The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet’s life support system. That is why, as an urgent first step, we propose that we establish a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism led by Nepal, India, and China. Through this mechanism, let us share satellite data and expertise.

Let us monitor dangerous glacial lakes. Let us strengthen joint early warning systems. And when disaster strikes, let us coordinate assistance across borders. Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation rather than a frontier of fragmented information. Remarkable for a least developed country, Nepal is already playing a global role exceeding its ecological share.

We have restored forest cover on nearly half of our territory. We are installing hydropower at a pace enough to power all our clean energy needs and displace dirty sources abroad. We are promoting electric mobility with an adoption rate to match parts of Europe. We are strengthening climate adaptation at the local level, and we shall do more to withstand the increasing intensity and frequency of climate disasters. But Nepal cannot build resilience alone against a crisis made worse by the failure of global governance.

Relief, Rehabilitation, Reconstruction — and Responsibility, Reparation, Resilience

This is why this assembly must note six words: “relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction,” and also “responsibility, reparation, resilience.” The first three are what we need after a disaster.

After opting to bat first, Hong Kong, China struggled to build momentum but posted 121 for 8 from their 20 overs. Hafeez Khan top-scored with 33, while Babar Hayat contributed 23 in a 51-run third-wicket partnership that briefly steadied the innings.

title: Nepal paying ‘colossal price’ for climate crisis after deadly floods - The Independent
description: Nepal paying ‘colossal price’ for climate crisis after deadly floods  The Independent
publisher.title: The Independent
full_article:
Nepalese prime minister Balendra Shah told the UN General Assembly that recent floods in Nepal which killed at least 1,400 people are a severe warning to the world about the accelerating climate crisis.

Mr Shah called for an urgent overhaul of international climate finance, stating that vulnerable nations facing disasters should not be forced to navigate complex bureaucratic mazes to receive aid.

Preliminary assessments indicate that Nepal suffered over $5bn (£3.7bn) in damage from the flooding, amounting to approximately 15 per cent of the nation's GDP.

The prime minister highlighted the injustice of the crisis, noting that Nepal contributes less than a tenth of one per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions yet suffers catastrophic consequences.

Nepal is seeking $20m from the global Loss and Damage Fund, but international responses remain severely underfunded, with US emergency aid covering less than one per cent of Nepal's total losses.

title: Sonoma fundraiser raises over $100,000 for Nepal flood relief - The Tourism Times
description: Sonoma fundraiser raises over $100,000 for Nepal flood relief  The Tourism Times
publisher.title: The Tourism Times
full_article:
KATHMANDU: A fundraising event organised by the Himalayan Sherpa Club of Sonoma and the California Sherpa Association has raised more than $100,000 for communities affected by the recent floods in Nepal.

The “Sonoma for Nepal: A Flood Relief Charity Dinner” was held at Sonoma Veterans Memorial Hall with support from the City of Sonoma. The organisers said $100,275 had been raised so far, with donations to remain open until the end of September.

The funds will be transferred to Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund through the California Sherpa Association after the campaign concludes and the final amount is determined, said association president Gombu Sherpa.

Hundreds of community members and dignitaries attended the event, with restaurants, wineries and volunteer organisations also joining the humanitarian initiative. Members of the Sherpa community offered Buddhist prayers for those who lost their lives in the floods.

A video showing the devastation caused by the August 26 floods along the Bhotekoshi-Trishuli corridors was also screened during the programme. People from different parts of the San Francisco Bay Area attended the event in solidarity with Nepal.

Sonoma Mayor Ron Wellander said the city continued to support its Nepali community, while US Representative Mike Thompson of California’s 4th Congressional District praised the Sherpa community’s efforts to support flood-affected communities in Nepal.

Pemba Sherpa, president of the Himalayan Sherpa Club of Sonoma, said the event reflected the continuing connection between the Nepali diaspora and their homeland. “Our bond with Nepal is getting stronger though we live miles away from the homeland,” he said.

For a change, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balen Shah was speaking. Addressing the UN General Assembly in New York, Shah made it clear where his priorities lay:

“I am told I am the youngest head of government to address this assembly this year. I did not come here to make that a story,” he said.

Wearing his trademark dark shades and black dhaka topi, he proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, led jointly by Nepal, India and China, for shared satellite data, glacial-lake monitoring and early warning.

This mechanism, according to Shah, would strengthen early-warning systems and cooperate during disasters.

“Climate change does not recognise borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports,” he said.

“The Bhotekoshi-Trisuli disaster was not just a local tragedy. It was a warning to the world. And I ask you today: have we really heard that warning?” he asked.

Thanking India and China for the relief they rendered in the wake of the floods, he underscored “We are not here to blame any country or government.”

That appeared to be a major step back from earlier remarks where he said “Nepal contributes less than 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse-gas emissions. We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it. For Nepal, climate catastrophe is also a development emergency.”

Shah estimated the damage caused by the floods at 10% of his country’s GDP (about $46 bn), and said initial recovery costs could exceed $5 billion. International assessments have pitched the damage at around $20 billion.

He sought “grant-based support” from the UN, saying Nepal should not have to take on loans to pay for flood relief work and reconstruction.

Nepali media, while giving full play to their prime minister’s remarks at the UN, also hoped that after returning home he would speak more to his people, parliament and party.

title: 56 Ukrainians Are Missing in Nepal Following Floods and a Landslide — Foreign Ministry - UA.NEWS
description: 56 Ukrainians Are Missing in Nepal Following Floods and a Landslide — Foreign Ministry  UA.NEWS
publisher.title: UA.NEWS
full_article:
The Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs has no information regarding confirmed Ukrainian fatalities resulting from the flood and landslide in Nepal. At this time, the fate of 56 Ukrainian citizens remains unknown; they are considered missing.

This was reported by the press service of the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The Ministry noted that as of September 25, the official number of missing and sought-after Ukrainian citizens stands at 56. No information regarding confirmed Ukrainian fatalities or injuries has been released.

The Ukrainian Embassy in China continues to transfer DNA data from the families of the missing citizens to the Chinese authorities.

Citing data from the relevant authorities in Nepal, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs adds that the statistics remain unchanged: 1,451 people have died, and 6,150 are considered missing. According to the Chinese side, 43 people have been confirmed dead, and 519 are considered missing (including 261 foreigners from 23 countries).

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs added that, regarding the disappearance of Ukrainian citizens as a result of the natural disaster, preliminary investigations have been launched in the relevant criminal cases involving 49 individuals, and the necessary measures have been taken.

The situation remains difficult due to the scale of the destruction. Ukrainian diplomats are taking steps to locate and identify 56 Ukrainian citizens. The case is under special supervision, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.

A man who lost his family in floods in Nepal says he struggles to accept that they are gone as he speaks of his heartbreak after returning from the country.

Pramod Poudel, 34, from Uckfield, East Sussex, travelled to Nepal after losing contact with his wife Sumitra, mother Tulisa, brother Pardip and uncle Madhav following the disaster. He says now he does not believe they will be found.

About 1,400 people died while more than 6,000 people are still missing following the disaster, according to official data.

He added: "It was very hard to see all of the people in my community, and all of the houses that have been destroyed.

"I don't know what the future holds now. I was away from my family for the last 15 or 16 years, and I want to stay closer to them now."

Flood waters caused devastation after hitting the Nepal-Tibet border on 26 August.

Scientists say the floods were caused by a collapse of rock wall and glacier ice near the peak of Langtang Lirung, a mountain on Nepal's side of the Himalayas.

Nepal began their Asian Games men’s cricket campaign with a five-wicket win over Afghanistan on Friday, while Hong Kong, China, revived their quarter-final hopes after beating Oman by 41 runs.

Hong Kong, China bounced back from their opening loss to Malaysia to beat Oman by 41 runs, while Nepal marked the start of their campaign with a comfortable victory over Afghanistan, who had beaten Japan in their opening match.

Afghanistan, opting to bat first, lost their top three batters for single-figure scores to slip to 16-3. Faisal Shinozada provided some stability with 30 from 33 balls as he and Najibullah Zadran put together a 39-run partnership.

Shinozada’s dismissal triggered another collapse, with Afghanistan slipping from 55-4 to 65-6. Zadran held firm for 30, while Nangeyalia Kharote added 17 as Afghanistan were bowled out for 102.

Nepal’s bowling effort was led by Lalit Rajbanshi and Kushal Bhurtel. Rajbanshi claimed 3-13 with the new ball, striking in each of his first three overs, while Bhurtel took four wickets for 21 runs and came close to a hat-trick.

Nepal’s chase began with a wobble as they slipped to 12-2, but captain Paudel and Sundeep Jora steadied the innings. Paudel remained unbeaten on 33, while Jora made 34 as Nepal moved steadily towards their target.

Nepal will face Japan on September 26 as they look to secure a place in the quarter-finals.

Oman’s chase never got going as Ayush Shukla claimed three wickets for 13 runs in his opening three overs. Shuaib Al Balushi made 20 from 26 balls, but Oman were eventually bowled out for 80 in the 12th over, with captain Sufyan Mehmood top-scoring with 26 from 35 balls.
